strengths: Comprehensive multi-expert annotation pipeline combining specialized models (speech, music, sound, acoustic properties) with LLM CoT reasoning, producing rich annotations with 22,595 vocabulary compared to 1,260-5,581 in existing benchmarks
Novel DATE metric design that addresses real limitations of existing metrics by combining tf-idf weighted semantic similarity (penalizing generic terms) with cross-sample discriminability scoring
Diverse 8-domain data coverage including mixed domains (speech+music, etc.) that better represents real-world acoustic scenarios compared to prior work
Extensive benchmark scale with 20,000 clips and 18 reference captions per clip, along with 100k+ QA pairs across well-designed cognitive skill categories
Clear experimental insights revealing model weaknesses (all models score 6.8-19.4% on acoustic properties assessment, performance collapses on mixed domains)
Thorough documentation with complete implementation details, model specifications, prompts, and architectural descriptions enabling reasonable reproducibility of experimental setup
weaknesses: Critical absence of human validation: No human evaluation of whether LLM-generated annotations are actually fine-grained or superior to manual annotations. Since all annotations come from single LLM (Deepseek-R1), systematic biases are unassessed and no inter-annotator agreement reported

Insufficient DATE metric validation: Correlation with human judgment not quantified; only visual CDF comparison with LLM-as-judge (which itself has moderate κ=0.43 for captions). No human studies demonstrating DATE aligns with human quality preferences

Incomplete reproducibility despite claims: Abstract states 'data and code are available at' with no actual URL/link provided. Quality control threshold (GLAP=6) is 'empirically set' without justification. Method for generating 3 caption variants unexplained

Inadequate limitations discussion: No analysis of LLM bias affecting model architecture preferences, dataset bias from ACAV100M, whether annotations reflect human understanding vs. LLM patterns, or failure modes. Limitations relegated to future work

Limited novelty: Benchmark construction and LLM-based annotation not novel (AutoACD, LPMusicCaps precedents exist). Main novelty in DATE metric and domain coverage is incremental. Work is primarily solid engineering rather than methodological advance

Weak metric validation analysis: Lacks ablation studies on DATE components (semantic similarity vs. discriminability contributions). Harmonic mean choice unexplained; no comparison with other aggregation methods. Cross-sample discriminability purely ranking-based with no sensitivity analysis

Insufficient experimental depth: No statistical significance testing of model differences, no error analysis beyond single Figure 5 example, no explanation for extreme caption-only underperformance (10-14 vs. 43+ for LALMs)

Missing ethical considerations: No fairness analysis for gender/age/accent recognition components, privacy implications for speech data, or discussion of potential misuse of fine-grained audio understanding

strengths: Addresses a genuine problem: existing benchmarks inadequately capture fine-grained audio understanding, and current metrics fail to distinguish between generic and detailed descriptions

Substantial scale and breadth: 20k samples with 18 reference captions per clip provides rich annotation compared to prior work; extended multi-domain coverage (8 domains including mixed) offers comprehensive evaluation

Reasonable annotation approach: combining multiple specialized expert models with CoT LLM reasoning is sensible for capturing multi-perspective annotations across speech, music, and acoustic properties

Thoughtful metric design: DATE's combination of tf-idf-weighted semantic similarity (to penalize generic terms) and cross-sample discriminability (to reward uniqueness) directly targets the stated problem
Comprehensive model evaluation: assessment of multiple model types (caption-only, speech-focused, general-purpose LALMs) with fine-grained breakdown reveals model specializations and limitations
Novel data source: using ACAV100M rather than relying solely on AudioSet/Clotho provides dataset diversity
weaknesses: Critical reproducibility gap: data and code availability marked as blank at submission; complex annotation pipeline with LLM prompt engineering (4+ pages) is difficult to reproduce; reliance on specific models/versions that may change; no code provided

Insufficient validation of core contribution: DATE metric validated on only one case study (Figure 5) with three examples; no correlation analysis with human judgment on fine-grained understanding; appendix shows LLM-as-judge reference metric has only moderate agreement (κ=0.43 for captions)

Heavy LLM annotation dependency without human grounding: entire benchmark generated by Deepseek-R1 CoT; no inter-annotator agreement, no human evaluation of sample annotations, no comparison with human-written descriptions; claim that LLM avoids coarse-grained descriptions is unsupported

Quality control methodology lacks rigor: GLAP threshold set empirically to 6 without sensitivity analysis; 'hallucination removal' mentioned but not detailed; rule-based filtering criteria inadequately explained; no ablation studies showing each component's impact

Questionable metric design choices: cross-sample discriminability (S_dis) measures distinguishability not accuracy—a response could be unique yet incorrect; harmonic mean weighting of S_sim and S_dis lacks justification; no ablation on weighting schemes

Limited novelty: annotation approach (expert models + LLM synthesis) is not new (AutoACD, LPMusicCaps); metric combines standard NLP techniques (tf-idf) with straightforward ranking-based discriminability; primary contribution is scale rather than methodological innovation

Annotation pipeline complexity without validation: dozens of components (Figure 3) create multiple failure points; arbitrary weighting scheme (0.4/0.4/0.2); no ablation studies identifying essential components; conflicting expert outputs resolved by unstated method

Modest model evaluation insights: results confirm expected findings (larger models better, mixed domains harder); no actionable insights for model improvement; no systematic error analysis; limited exploration of what models fundamentally fail to understand

Presentation and clarity issues: Dense paper with complex components not clearly explained; Figure 1 too crowded; key details missing (are reference captions LLM-generated or manual? What exactly is hallucination removal?); notation inconsistencies in metric section

Incomplete ethical analysis: dataset includes sensitive speaker characteristics (gender, age, accent, emotion); no discussion of demographic bias in model evaluation or potential biases in LLM annotations; use of speaker attributes without fairness analysis

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important problem: existing benchmarks reward generic descriptions, failing to distinguish detailed from vague outputs in audio understanding tasks

Comprehensive and well-designed annotation pipeline combining specialized expert models (speech, music, sound, acoustic properties) with Chain-of-Thought LLM reasoning; systematic quality control with multiple filtering stages
Extended multi-domain coverage (8 domains including mixed combinations like speech+music+sound) enables evaluation of complex acoustic scenes, going beyond existing benchmarks
Novel data source (ACAV100M) provides genuine diversity; vocabulary size (22,595) is 4-17x larger than existing benchmarks, demonstrating improved lexical richness
DATE metric is intuitive and practical, demonstrably superior to FENSE in distinguishing high-quality from generic descriptions (CDF analysis shows 46 vs. 30 median score gap for Right vs. Wrong)

Comprehensive evaluation reveals actionable insights: architecture/training matter more than scale; systematic biases toward event recognition over acoustic properties (6.8-19.4 DATE for content-unrelated tasks)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed prompts (Appendix C), complete model lists, implementation details, and commitment to release code/data
High-quality benchmark construction at scale: 20k audio clips, 18 reference captions per clip (3 variants × 6 categories), 100k+ QA pairs spanning 6 cognitive levels
Clear, well-written presentation with effective motivation and comprehensive documentation of methodology
weaknesses: No human evaluation or inter-annotator agreement study for LLM-generated annotations; Appendix E validates LLM-as-judge as an evaluator but not the quality of LLM-generated ground truth

DATE metric lacks ablation studies on key design choices: no justification for harmonic mean vs. alternatives, equal weighting of semantic similarity and discriminability, or tf-idf scheme; no comparison with simpler baselines

Arbitrary design choices without justification: weighting scheme for caption categories (0.4/0.4/0.2) and Long/Short (0.8/0.2) appear ad-hoc; GLAP filtering threshold (6) empirically set with minimal discussion; equal weighting in QA scoring may not reflect cognitive importance

Limited experimental depth: only 4-5 models evaluated, no ablation studies on annotation pipeline components, no analysis of which annotation categories are most reliable, and shallow error analysis (low scores 20-60% raise questions about ground truth vs. model capability)

Missing evidence of practical utility: no demonstration that DATE actually improves downstream model development or that it produces materially different model rankings than LLM-as-judge on full benchmark
Incomplete technical documentation: percentage of samples failing quality control filters not reported, sensitivity to LLM hyperparameters unexplored, and mechanics of hallucination removal unclear
Cross-sample discriminability metric assumes optimal batch composition; sensitivity to batch selection and how it applies in streaming/online settings unexplored
Missing URL for code/data release in main manuscript; typo 'avaiable' instead of 'available' on page 1

strengths: Comprehensive multi-expert annotation pipeline with rigorous validation: 82.7% win rate vs. generic descriptions, 56.9% comparable to human references, and only 3.4% strict error rate
Large-scale benchmark (20k samples) with extended multi-domain coverage including mixed modalities, significantly larger than prior work (1-10k samples)
Novel DATE metric specifically designed for fine-grained audio evaluation, combining semantic similarity with cross-sample discriminability and showing clear advantages over FENSE and BLEU
Thorough experimental evaluation of 32 models with fine-grained analysis revealing insights (speech-centric bias, hallucination in silent segments) and proper statistical testing
Strong methodological rigor: bootstrap stability analysis (CV < 1%), sensitivity analysis (Kendall's τ = 0.92), and compelling alignment between DATE and human preferences (90.9 vs. 49.3)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: each component (expert models, LLM-CoT, embedding metrics) uses existing techniques; contribution is primarily in engineering and dataset construction rather than methodological innovation

Annotation pipeline concerns: acknowledged residual noise from expert hallucinations particularly in non-speech categories, unexplored LLM-CoT failure modes, lack of ablation studies on pipeline components, and arbitrary GLAP similarity threshold (6)

DATE metric design gaps: no ablation justifying harmonic mean over alternatives, acknowledged sensitivity to test set diversity (discriminability unreliable on homogeneous corpora), insensitivity to entity swaps, and missing comparisons with other discriminability-based metrics

Significant scope limitations: 10-second clips only (acknowledged as insufficient for long-range reasoning), English-language only, no transfer learning analysis showing whether gains generalize to older benchmarks or other domains

Methodological gaps: no inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ) reported for 700 expert REL evaluations, weighting choices (0.6/0.3/0.1) follow dataset composition rather than principled justification, LLM-as-Judge reference metric has only moderate reliability (κ=0.43)

strengths: Comprehensive multi-perspective annotation scheme with 18 references per clip across 6 well-motivated subcategories providing richer supervision than prior benchmarks
Extensive human validation with 150 A/B preference pairs and 700 expert REL audits, including per-category breakdown and detailed inter-rater statistics (Appendices F.1-F.2)
Large-scale empirical evaluation of 32 models with granular performance breakdowns that reveal interpretable patterns (speech-centric bias, acoustic property weakness, discriminability disparities)
DATE metric design combining embedding-level TF-IDF semantic similarity with cross-sample discriminability is novel and addresses real limitations of existing metrics like FENSE
Thorough documentation of methodology including detailed LLM prompts, expert model specifications, quality control procedures, and bootstrap stability analyses
weaknesses: Fundamental data quality concern: only ~10% sample survival through filtering pipeline due to expert model hallucinations; while multi-stage filtering helps, 700/20K (~3.5%) human audit coverage with 3.4% error rate [95% CI: 2.3%-5.1%] leaves ~5% plausible error rate; no audit of QA pair quality

Significant domain variance in annotation quality (Table F.3: Speech REL=4.10 vs Sound REL=3.45, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.267) indicates pipeline effectiveness is domain-dependent, yet all weighted equally in final score; speech-centric bias appears partly in benchmark construction (6:3:1 weighting) not purely in model limitations
Evaluation methodology bias: Audio Flamingo 2 used in annotation pipeline, Audio Flamingo 3 evaluated—acknowledged but creates potential inflation of proprietary model scores

DATE metric has unresolved fundamental limitation: cross-sample discriminability component depends critically on test set diversity and composition, limiting applicability to homogeneous datasets; acknowledged but not addressed; limited empirical validation with modest CDF separation from FENSE baseline and alignment with human judgment based only on 150 pairs

Limited novelty: expert model + LLM annotation pipeline is increasingly standard (AutoACD, LPMusicCaps); multi-domain coverage is incremental; multiple references per clip was used in Clotho; TF-IDF + ranking components are straightforward; empirical insights (speech bias, acoustic property difficulty) are unsurprising

Incomplete QA validation: only 5 QA pairs per clip with no quality audits provided (Appendix F only validates captions); extreme performance variance (Table 3: Quality Assessment scores range 18.7-39.3, suggesting potential annotation issues); unclear if these pairs are representative

No cross-benchmark generalization analysis: missing comparison of model performance on MECAT vs AudioCaps/Clotho; no investigation of whether MECAT provides fundamentally different evaluation than existing benchmarks

DATE metric ablation studies absent: embedding-level TF-IDF (Appendix E) is complex but not validated against simpler alternatives (standard embeddings, other embedding models); no component importance analysis; using LLM-as-judge for validation (Appendix H) paradoxically undermines DATE value proposition

Scoring scheme relies on heuristically set weights (0.4/0.4/0.2, 0.8/0.2) despite sensitivity analysis showing stability; alternative weightings (Table F.4) should influence main results not just appendix

Bootstrap stability shows concerning variance for smaller domains (Pure-Sound CV=1.04%, Pure-Music CV=0.77% at full scale; Pure-Sound CV=18.62% at 1% sampling), suggesting unreliable DATE scores on smaller/diverse subsets

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates concrete limitations of existing benchmarks (simplistic annotations, monolithic perspectives, metric inadequacy) with compelling examples

Novel benchmark at scale: 20k samples from new data source (ACAV100M) with extended multi-domain coverage (8 domains including combinations) and rich multi-perspective annotations (18 references per clip)
Rigorous annotation pipeline: Sophisticated multi-stage approach with specialized expert models, CoT LLM reasoning, conflict resolution, and dual-layer human validation (A/B testing + expert audit)

Novel DATE metric: Addresses genuine limitation of existing metrics; combines semantic similarity with cross-sample discriminability; validated with 41-point margin against human preferences (90.9 vs 49.3)

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 17 captioning and 15 QA models; reveals actionable insights (speech-centric bias, acoustic property weakness, hallucination in silence); stability analysis shows Kendall's τ = 0.92 across weighting scenarios

Thorough validation: Multiple human evaluation rounds (150 A/B pairs with >94% win rate over wrong captions; 700-sample expert audit with 85.3% acceptable scores); bootstrap stability analysis (CV <1% at full scale)
Strong reproducibility: Detailed prompts in appendices, comprehensive methodology documentation, promised public release of code and data, clear human evaluation protocols
weaknesses: Circular dependency with model architectures: Audio Flamingo 2 explicitly used in annotation pipeline; Audio Flamingo 3 then evaluated on benchmark. Creates potential bias that could inflate LALM performance metrics, concerning for reproducibility by independent researchers

Data quality ceiling despite filtering: 90% rejection rate suggests upstream model issues or overly restrictive standards; residual hallucination acknowledged; non-speech categories show meaningful quality variance (Speech REL=3.98 vs Sound=3.69); 3.4% strict error rate represents ~680 erroneous annotations

Limited temporal scope: 10-second clips prioritize clip-local understanding; acknowledged as complementary but real constraint for applications requiring temporal reasoning over longer sequences; generalization to longer audio unclear

DATE metric limitations: Inherits embedding-based similarity weaknesses (insensitive to entity swaps); cross-sample discriminability acknowledged as most informative when test set diverse — performance on homogeneous corpora unknown; requires full test set access for ranking

Heuristic design choices: ScoreCap weights (6:3:1) based on ACAV100M prevalence rather than theoretical optimality; QA difficulty distribution (25/35/25/15 split) prescribed without justification; while weighting sensitivity analysis shows stability, arbitrary baseline weights remain

QA task validation gaps: Human evaluation focuses primarily on captioning; QA validation less comprehensive; difficulty distribution enforcement unclear; no human evaluation confirming whether QA pairs test intended cognitive skills

Model evaluation fairness concerns: Different prompts for different model families (Table I); heterogeneous architectures compared without normalization; Phi-4-Multimodal included despite not being audio-native; no ablation on prompt engineering sensitivity

Incomplete statistical rigor: Some claims lack confidence intervals (model rankings in Tables 2-3); bootstrap stability thorough for DATE but not other metrics; per-category audit shows variance but lacks multiple-comparison correction
